title: Forest at the Wilder Kaiser, Tyrol, 360×180, 160620, ako — consumer 360 (CC BY-SA 4.0)
description: Mountain forest at the Wilder Kaiser (Tyrol) as a 360° panorama — forest application of the equirectangular input with openly licensed data. 360° equirectangular panorama taken with a consumer 360° camera. Source: Wikimedia Commons, Ansgar Koreng, CC BY-SA 4.0. Scaled to 4096×2048.

markers.label: Region & Standort
markers.title: Region & Standort
markers.subtitle: Northern Limestone Alps · Wilder Kaiser · Tyrol
markers.body:
The Wilder Kaiser is a rugged limestone massif of the Kaisergebirge in Tyrol (Austria). The panorama shows a montane mixed mountain forest at its wooded foot — the typical altitudinal zone between valley and dwarf-pine belt.

The climate is cool and humid: much precipitation, a short growing season, long snow cover. Such stands often serve as protection forest against rockfall, avalanches and erosion on steep slopes.
markers.note: Climate/relief values typical for the site; Tyrol figures measured (Austrian NFI). Site-typical reference values for a mixed mountain forest of the Northern Limestone Alps — no field survey at this panorama.

markers.label: Ground
markers.title: Ground
markers.subtitle: Kalkalpine Rendzina / Terra fusca
markers.body:
On the Wetterstein limestone and dolomite of the Limestone Alps, shallow, stony soils develop. The mineral soil is base-rich (much calcium), the humus layer acidic.

The rock is highly permeable and karstified — water seeps away quickly, so summer dry spells can occur despite high precipitation. The pale limestones visible along the path in the foreground reveal the bedrock.
markers.note: Site-typical reference values for a mixed mountain forest of the Northern Limestone Alps — no field survey at this panorama.

markers.label: Tree species
markers.title: Tree species
markers.subtitle: Fichten-Tannen-Buchen-Bergmischwald
markers.body:
The natural forest community of the montane Limestone Alps is the spruce–fir–beech forest (Abieti-Fagetum). The three species complement each other ecologically: Norway spruce dominates economically, the shade-tolerant silver fir roots deeply and stabilises, beech improves humus and soil life.

Clearly visible: the dark, columnar spruces on the right, with the lighter foliage of beech in between. Valuable broadleaves such as sycamore maple and single larches are mixed in.
markers.note: Tyrol shares and forest community measured/mapped (Austrian NFI, BFW). The site-typical mixture of this stand is illustrative.

markers.label: Diameter distribution
markers.title: Diameter distribution
markers.subtitle: Trees per ha by DBH class
markers.body:
The distribution has one peak in the middle (bell-shaped) and is grouped around the mean diameter. This is typical of an approximately even-aged stand in the mature phase — most trees grew up together and are of similar thickness today.

The small foot in the thin classes is beginning regeneration and suppressed trees.
markers.note: Distribution modelled for the site (no local survey); the share of large timber is a real Austrian NFI finding.

markers.label: Regeneration
markers.title: Regeneration
markers.subtitle: Natural regeneration in the stand's shade
markers.body:
Under the closed canopy, shade-tolerant silver fir, beech and Norway spruce germinate in half-shade. This natural regeneration builds the next forest generation as soon as the canopy opens through harvest or disturbance.

The bottleneck is usually browsing by deer: silver fir in particular is heavily browsed by roe and red deer and drops out of the mixed forest without hunting or protection.
markers.note: Browsing/bark-stripping damage measured (Austrian NFI, Austria-wide). Regeneration picture of this stand typical for the site.
